explanations.explanation: That's what Jesus says, friend: after that tribulation, the sun will be darkened. He says it plainly, so there's nothing to decode. The lights go dim before anything else happens. Sit with that for a second, because Jesus doesn't rush it.
Standing still sounds dramatic, I'll give you that. But Jesus doesn't say the sun stops. He says it will be darkened. The sun doesn't pause in this verse, it goes dim.

Hotter is a fair guess, since my oven turns up the heat when I want a bigger sizzle. But Jesus goes the opposite direction. He says the sun will be darkened, and that's the whole picture. Less light, not more.

I see why you'd think the moon picks up the slack. Somebody has to cover the night shift, right? But Jesus says the moon will not give its light either. So the sun goes dark and the moon doesn't step in.
Right, friend. Jesus says the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light. Neither one is working. The text says both go dark, so no backup light is coming from the moon.
Yes. Jesus says the stars will fall from the sky. That's the same sky where one of my stars lights up for every finished cookie box, so I read this line twice. Jesus says it, so I take it seriously.
Close, but Jesus does say it. In His words, the stars will fall from the sky. It's right there in verse 25, right after the sun and moon go dark. I keep my eyes on the sky just like He says.

That's it, baker. Jesus says the powers of the heavens will be shaken. Whatever those powers are, they don't stay steady. It's like a counter when somebody slams the oven door, except this is the heavens.
Restored would be a gentler ending, but that's not what Jesus says here. He says the powers of the heavens will be shaken. Shaken is the word, not fixed up.
Standing guard would make them sound steady and calm. Jesus says the opposite: the powers of the heavens will be shaken. Nobody's holding a post in this verse. Everything's rattling.

I get the thought, because Elijah (the prophet who spoke for God to Israel) is a big name. But look at what Jesus says. They will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds. Elijah isn't in this verse at all.

That's right, friend. In all that dark, Jesus says they will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds. He doesn't mention Elijah anywhere in this passage. The person coming in the clouds is the Son of Man, and that's Jesus' name for Himself.
Yes, with great power and glory. That's how Jesus says it: they will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds with great power and glory. The sky goes dark, and then comes that. Not a quiet entrance.
A horse makes a grand picture, doesn't it? But Mark doesn't give Jesus a horse here. He says the Son of Man comes in the clouds with great power and glory. The clouds are the ride in this verse.

explanations.answer: Hidden in a cloud of smoke
explanations.explanation: Smoke makes me think of my oven on a rough day. But Jesus doesn't say the Son of Man comes hidden. They will see Him coming in the clouds with great power and glory. Seen, not hidden.
Gather is the word. Jesus says He will send out the angels to gather His elect. The angels are sent out for one job in this verse, and that job is gathering.
I can see why that one pops up, but it's not what Jesus says in this verse. He sends out the angels to gather His elect. The job here is gathering.
Warning is a good job for a messenger, and Jesus has done plenty of warning in this teaching. But in this verse, the angels are sent out to gather His elect. The word is gather.
Yes, from the four winds. Jesus says from the four winds, from the ends of the earth to the ends of heaven. That's a wide reach. The gathering goes from one far edge to the other.

Israel is a natural guess, since Jesus is talking to Israelites. But He doesn't name any one land. He says from the four winds, from the ends of the earth to the ends of heaven. The reach is much wider than one country.

Jerusalem is the city on everybody's mind in this teaching, so I get the guess. But Jesus doesn't mention it in this verse. The angels gather from the four winds, from the ends of the earth to the ends of heaven. That's way bigger than one city.

explanations.answer: They get tender and sprout leaves
explanations.explanation: That's it. Jesus says that when the fig branches become tender and sprout leaves, you know summer is near. The branches tell you before the season shows up. It's a sign you can read just by looking.

explanations.answer: They drop all of their fruit
explanations.explanation: Dropping everything sounds like a lot happening at once. But Jesus doesn't talk about fruit falling in this lesson. He says the branches become tender and sprout leaves. Leaves coming in are the sign.

explanations.answer: They dry out and start to crack
explanations.explanation: Dry and cracking is what happens to my cookies when I leave them out too long. That's a snack problem, not a season sign. Jesus says the fig branches become tender and sprout leaves. Soft and leafy, not dry.
Summer is right. Jesus says that as soon as the branches become tender and sprout leaves, you know that summer is near. The tree gives the early notice. Anybody watching it can tell.
Winter would be a cold turn, but Jesus doesn't say that. He says leaves on tender branches mean that summer is near. Leaves are on their way in, not out.
Autumn is a nice guess, since leaves come up in that season too. But Jesus names a different season in this lesson. When the branches sprout leaves, He says, you know that summer is near.

explanations.answer: He is near right at the door
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Jesus says that when you see these things happening, know that He is near, right at the door. He turns the fig tree into a lesson about the very things He's been describing. The tree shows summer coming, and the signs show Him near.

explanations.answer: They still have plenty of time
explanations.explanation: Plenty of time sounds comfortable, like a long afternoon with no timer going. But that isn't what Jesus says. When they see these things happening, they should know that He is near, right at the door. Near is the word.

The temple was on the disciples' minds at the start of this teaching, so I see the link. But Jesus says nothing about it being rebuilt in these verses. He says that when they see these things happening, they should know that He is near, right at the door.

True. Jesus tells them to learn a lesson from the fig tree: leaves mean summer is near. Then He says that when they see these things happening, they should know that He is near, right at the door. Watching the branches and watching the signs work the same way.

This one's true, friend. Jesus opens with 'learn this lesson from the fig tree' and uses the sprouting leaves to show how to read the season. Then He applies it: when you see these things happening, know that He is near. The signs are read the way you'd read the tree.

Yes, never. Jesus says heaven and earth will pass away, but His words will never pass away. That puts His words on firmer ground than the sky and the ground itself. Nothing in the whole passage is steadier.
Not quite. Jesus says it the other way around: heaven and earth will pass away, but His words will never pass away. His words don't go first. They outlast the biggest things there are.
Forgetting is how most things go. Even recipes get lost. But Jesus says His words will never pass away. They stay, even when heaven and earth don't.
That's it. Jesus says no one knows about that day or hour, but only the Father. So there's no guessing from me, and no guessing from anybody else. The knowing belongs to the Father.
You'd think the angels, who are in heaven, would be in the know. But Jesus says no one knows about that day or hour, not even the angels in heaven. Only the Father knows.

The high priest is a big name, but Jesus doesn't mention him in these verses. He says no one knows about that day or hour, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father. The list stops at the Father.

True. Jesus says it in His own words: no one knows about that day or hour, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father. I'm just repeating what He said. The text states it plainly.

It's in the text, friend. Jesus says no one knows about that day or hour, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father. 'Nor the Son' is right there in His words. Only the Father is named as knowing.

explanations.answer: Be on guard and stay alert
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Jesus says, 'Be on your guard and stay alert! For you do not know when the appointed time will come.' Not knowing the time is exactly why He says to stay ready. That's why my ovens stay warm.

explanations.answer: Wait for a prophet to tell them
explanations.explanation: A prophet giving a heads-up would be handy, like a text before the guests arrive. But Jesus doesn't send them looking for one. He tells them to be on their guard and stay alert. The watching is theirs to do.
Resting sounds nice, I won't lie. But Jesus says the opposite. He tells them to be on their guard and stay alert, because they do not know when the appointed time will come.
That's it. The man puts each servant in charge of his own task. Everybody gets a job, so nobody is standing around with nothing to do. Even before the master is gone, the work is handed out.
A bag of silver shows up in some of Jesus' other teachings, but not in this picture. Here the man puts each servant in charge of his own task. It's about work, not money.
A key makes sense for a house. I even knew a key once that never found its door. But Jesus doesn't mention one in this picture. The man puts each servant in charge of his own task.
Watch is the word. The man instructs the doorkeeper to keep watch. That job sits at the door, so the doorkeeper's eyes stay open for the master coming home.
Quiet sounds like a fine order for a night guard. But the man doesn't tell the doorkeeper to keep quiet. He tells him to keep watch.
Busy fits the servants who got their own tasks, so I see the mix-up. But the doorkeeper gets a different instruction. The man tells him to keep watch.

That's right. Jesus lists evening, midnight, when the rooster crows, and the morning. Put those together and they cover the stretch from evening to morning. The master could come back at any one of them.
The morning is on Jesus' list, but He starts earlier than that. He names evening, midnight, when the rooster crows, and the morning. That whole run is the night through to the morning.
That's the afternoon stretch, and none of Jesus' times land there. He names evening, midnight, when the rooster crows, and the morning. It's a night watch, not an afternoon one.

That's the warning. Jesus says, 'Otherwise, he may arrive without notice and find you sleeping.' The danger isn't only that the master comes back, it's that he finds you asleep. That's why He says to keep watch.
An unlocked door sounds like a real problem. But Jesus doesn't say that here. He warns that the master may arrive without notice and find you sleeping.
Lamps going out come up in another one of Jesus' teachings, but not in this one. Here He warns that the master may arrive without notice and find you sleeping.

I can see why you'd think that, since He's been talking to a small group on the Mount of Olives. But Jesus widens it at the end. He says, “…what I say to you, I say to everyone: Keep watch!” The call reaches past those four.

Right, friend. Jesus says, “…what I say to you, I say to everyone: Keep watch!” It starts with the ones sitting in front of Him, but it doesn't stop there. The call to keep watch is for everyone, and that includes you.
